passages.t: The drought, and a prayer God will not accept
passages.happening:
The word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah about the drought (verse 1). Judah mourns, and a cry goes up from Jerusalem (verse 2). ‘The nobles send their servants for water; they go to the cisterns, but find no water’ (verse 3), and their jars come back empty. ‘The ground is cracked because no rain has fallen on the land’ (verse 4). The farmers cover their heads. ‘Even the doe in the field deserts her newborn fawn because there is no grass’ (verse 5). Wild donkeys stand on the bare heights panting like jackals (verse 6).

Then a prayer. ‘Although our iniquities testify against us, O LORD, act for the sake of Your name’ (verse 7). ‘O Hope of Israel, its Savior in times of distress, why are You like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who stays but a night?’ (verse 8). Why is he like a warrior powerless to save? They are called by his name (verse 9).

God answers that they love to wander and have not held back their feet (verse 10). He tells Jeremiah not to pray for the people's welfare (verse 11). Though they fast and bring offerings, he will not accept them, but will finish them with sword, famine and plague (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Judah was a land of rain-fed farming. It had no great river like the Nile or the Euphrates to water its fields, so failed winter rains meant failed harvests and, in time, famine. Jerusalem's water came from springs and from cisterns, chambers cut into rock to store rain. When the cisterns were dry, even the nobles had nothing.

Covering the head was a sign of grief and shame, as when David climbed the Mount of Olives with his head covered. Public fasting and offerings were the ordinary ways Israel sought God in a national crisis.

The doe abandoning her fawn is a picture of nature itself breaking down. A deer was known for tenderness to its young.

The chapter does not say when the drought happened, and no outside record fixes it.
passages.later: Joel describes the same suffering of the animals: ‘Even the beasts of the field pant for You, for the streams of water have dried up’ (Joel 1:20). In Elijah's day God ended a drought when he said, ‘I will send rain upon the face of the earth’ (1 Kings 18:1).
passages.hard:
If God refuses the people's fasting and prayer, what hope is there for anyone who prays?

The refusal can sound as though God shuts his ears to sincere prayer. But the chapter gives reasons. The prayer in verses 7 to 9 is a real confession in form, yet verse 10 says the people still love to wander, and their prophets were telling them no disaster would come. The refusal is aimed at a nation that wanted rescue from the consequences while keeping what caused them. It is a refusal to prevent a judgment already decided, not a refusal ever to hear. The same book promises that when the people seek God with all their heart in exile, they will find him (29:13).

A drought then, or a disaster now, is not a sign that God has rejected the people it falls on.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: The people prayed to God as their hope while loving to wander. Ask whether your prayers ask God to rescue you from consequences you are not willing to leave. And ask what it would look like to seek God with all your heart.

passages.t: Lying prophets, tears, and a people still praying
passages.happening:
Jeremiah protests that the prophets are telling the people they will see no sword or famine, but lasting peace (verse 13). ‘The prophets are prophesying lies in My name,’ God answers (verse 14). He did not send them. They prophesy false visions and the deceit of their own minds. The prophets who say no sword or famine will come will die by sword and famine (verse 15), and the people who listen will lie unburied in the streets (verse 16).

Jeremiah is to say that his eyes overflow with tears day and night, ‘for the virgin daughter of my people has been shattered by a crushing blow’ (verse 17). In the country he sees the slain, and in the city those ravaged by famine; prophet and priest wander in a land they do not know (verse 18).

The people pray again. ‘Have You rejected Judah completely? Do You despise Zion?’ (verse 19). ‘We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, the guilt of our fathers’ (verse 20). For the sake of his name, they ask God not to break his covenant (verse 21). ‘Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain?’ (verse 22). Only God can. ‘So we put our hope in You, for You have done all these things’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The prophets who promised lasting peace were real and influential. They probably drew on a genuine tradition, the promise that God had chosen Zion and would defend it, which had seemed to come true when Jerusalem was spared from Assyria in Hezekiah's day. Jeremiah's conflict with them grows through the book, most of all with Hananiah in chapter 28.

The chapter ends with the people still praying, and with a true confession: idols cannot bring rain; only the LORD can. Whatever God's answer, the Bible keeps the prayer.

Rain was the clearest test between the LORD and Baal, who was believed to send it. Verse 22 settles the question.
passages.later: James points to Elijah, who ‘prayed earnestly that it would not rain’ (James 5:17), as an example of prayer. Jeremiah later writes to the exiles, ‘You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart’ (Jeremiah 29:13).
passages.asks: The people ended by saying their hope was in God alone. Ask what you hope in when the rain does not come. And ask which voices around you promise peace without asking anything of you.
